title: Preity Zinta Just Sued Google and Meta. The Reason Should Terrify Every Woman Online.
excerpt: The Bollywood star and IPL team co-owner is taking AI-generated deepfakes to Bombay High Court — and she's not the first celebrity forced to fight back this year.
body:
The first thing you need to know is that **Preity Zinta** didn't ask for this fight. Nobody does.

On July 3, the actress — beloved for two decades of Bollywood cinema, from the dimpled heartbreak of *Kal Ho Naa Ho* to the fierce independence of *Veer-Zaara* — walked into the Bombay High Court with a civil suit that names some of the biggest companies on the planet. Google LLC. **Meta Platforms Inc.** Domain registrars. And a list of unidentified individuals who have been manufacturing her likeness using artificial intelligence.

The suit, *Preity Zinta v. Google LLC & Ors.*, lays out a disturbing inventory: AI-generated deepfake videos, morphed images, fake advertisements, chatbot-style interactions that simulate her personality — all circulating freely across YouTube, Instagram, and Facebook. None of it authorized. None of it real. All of it convincing enough that her legal team, led by senior advocate **Venkatesh Dhond**, told the court that the quality of these deepfakes is "steadily improving."

Let that sink in. The fakes are getting better, faster than the platforms can catch them.

## The Courtroom

**Justice Madhav Jamdar** heard the case on a single bench. Dhond pressed for urgent ex parte orders — immediate takedowns of every identified piece of infringing content, plus broader "John Doe" directions against unknown future infringers. He argued that Zinta's personality rights, moral rights, and right to privacy were all being violated.

Google and Meta's lawyers didn't exactly oppose her. They told the court they were willing to delete specific links carrying morphed or obscene content — but pushed back hard against any blanket monitoring order. Some of the flagged URLs, they argued, don't actually contain infringing material. A domain name registrar pointed out that it merely registers names and can't police what's hosted on social media platforms.

Justice Jamdar's response was measured but pointed. He acknowledged that protective orders are warranted, but insisted any mechanism must be "calibrated" — targeting the objectionable material without accidentally taking down legitimate content. He asked all parties to confer and come back with a practical takedown protocol.

The next hearing is **July 6** — tomorrow.

## She's Not Alone

Preity Zinta is the latest, but hardly the first, Indian celebrity to take the legal route against AI-generated content this year. In June, the Delhi High Court granted relief to Telugu star **Naga Chaitanya**, ordering the removal of AI-generated pornographic and defamatory content using his likeness. In May, Kannada actress **Rukmini Vasanth** broke her silence on viral AI-generated images and initiated legal action of her own.

The pattern is unmistakable: deepfake technology has become cheap, accessible, and terrifyingly effective — and the people it targets most are women in the public eye.

> "The quality of the deepfakes is steadily improving." — Senior Advocate Venkatesh Dhond, representing Preity Zinta

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs who grew up watching Preity Zinta light up every frame she entered — from the college corridors of *Koi... Mil Gaya* to the cricket stadiums where she co-owns the **Punjab Kings** — this story cuts close. It's a reminder that the digital world doesn't respect borders, and neither do the people exploiting AI to manufacture someone else's face.

The case also raises a question that extends well beyond Bollywood: if someone with Preity Zinta's resources, legal team, and public profile has to go to the High Court to get fake content taken down, what chance does an ordinary woman have?

India's legal framework is still catching up. There is no comprehensive deepfake-specific legislation on the books yet, though the Information Technology Act and various personality-rights doctrines are being stretched to cover the gap. Courts are essentially writing the rules in real time, case by case.

Justice Jamdar's eventual order could set an important precedent — not just for celebrities, but for anyone whose face has been stolen by a machine.

The hearing resumes Monday. Preity Zinta will be watching. So should the rest of us.
